corneille-oeuvres-marty-laveaux-t2:
Tome two of the Marty-Laveaux Corneille appeared in the same French great-writers series. The series ran under the direction of Ad. Regnier, a member of the Institute. Like tome one, it keeps the old spelling and numbers verses by fives.

Here the edition reaches the summit of Corneille's career. Le Cid, Horace, Cinna, and Polyeucte belong to these peak years, by the v1 account. His figures choose honor over love and duty over life itself. They speak in verse of unmatched grandeur and pride. Schoolchildren memorized this Corneille for three centuries, the poet of the will at its grandest and most heroic.
kindred-sayings-part2:
Part Two of the Kindred Sayings appeared in Rhys Davids's English in 1922. The Samyutta Nikaya's themed discourses carry forward from the first part. Causation, the elements, and the aggregates anchor this second stretch.

The Buddha teaches how things arise from causes and pass away. Monks, lay folk, and gods all pose their questions in the talks. Verse and prose mix in the old collection's varied, lively manner. The Pali canon's deep thought reaches English in pioneer form here. Readers feel the system of early Buddhism lock into place, piece by piece here. The part's talks on causes reward slow, thoughtful reading.
quesnay-physiocratie-1768-part2:
Part 2 of Dupont's Physiocratie, issued in 1768, carries the collection beyond Quesnay's own maxims. The first part had stated the master's first principles; the sequel shows the school at work. Dupont, the school's great organizer, printed the followers beside the founder so the doctrine could be judged whole.

The writings here work out nature's rule in trade and tillage: free export of grain, a single tax on land, and the removal of guilds and tolls. The authors argue case by case, answering critics of the new science of political economy. Read together, the two parts preserve the first movement of economists speaking for itself, in its own journals and terms. The volume is key evidence for how a school of thought organizes, publishes, and fights for a hearing.
stendhal-lucien-leuwen-t2:
Part two of Lucien Leuwen opens with a sly address to the kind reader. Stendhal warns that Paris tempts him toward sharp personal satire. Such satire, he argues, would kill the reader's care for his other figures, so he resists it.

Lucien now moves in Paris and in the machinery of government offices. High hopes meet cold self-interest in the halls of power. Stendhal's irony cuts bureaucrats and climbers with unmatched precision here. The novel stayed unfinished, yet its two parts form a great portrait of ambition in French letters. No one since has skewered office life and social climbing with quite his light, dry touch.
